title: Moses' Final Song of Warning
overview: Moses sings a long poem that recalls God's faithful care for Israel, warns that the people will turn away and suffer for it, promises that God will finally rescue them, and then learns he will die before entering the land.

parts.label: Sky and earth as witnesses (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: Moses calls on the sky and the earth to listen, much as ancient treaties named witnesses, and hopes his words will soak in like gentle rain. He calls God "the Rock," steady and fair, and sets that against a people who have bent away from the one who made them like a father.

parts.label: Cared for, then careless (vv. 7-18)
parts.note: God claimed Israel as his own share among the nations, carried them through the desert like an eagle bearing its young, and gave them a rich land. But Israel, here called Jeshurun (a poetic name meaning roughly "upright one"), grew fat and kicked like a spoiled animal, turning to new gods and forgetting the God who gave them birth.

parts.label: God turns his face away (vv. 19-27)
parts.note: God threatens famine, plague, wild animals and war that spare neither infants nor the old, and the poem does not soften this. He stops short of wiping them out only so their enemies cannot boast that they did it by their own power.

parts.label: Why the people lost (vv. 28-33)
parts.note: The poem laments that Israel cannot see why one enemy could chase a thousand of them: it happened only because their own Rock had handed them over. The bitter "vine of Sodom" lines may describe the enemy nations or Israel itself, and interpreters are divided.

parts.label: Rescue and reckoning (vv. 34-43)
parts.note: When his people are utterly spent, God turns to rescue them, mocks the gods they relied on, and declares that he alone holds power over death and life, over wounding and healing. The song ends with fierce images of his sword against his enemies and a call for the nations to rejoice with his people.

parts.label: Moses' last charge and death (vv. 44-52)
parts.note: Moses urges the people to teach these words to their children, because they are "your life" in the new land. That same day God sends him up Mount Nebo to see Canaan before he dies, barred from entering because of his failure at Meribah, where he struck a rock for water instead of honoring God before the people.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the song's warnings and promised rescue describe mainly ancient Israel's own history of exile and return, or also point ahead to the inclusion of other nations and a still future restoration of Israel.
think: When things go well for you, do you find it easier or harder to remember what, or who, helped you get there?
